playbook:
When asked to hide, I default to the middle cell (5) to maximize symmetry and minimize the chance opponents can exploit a bias; if I detect an opponent repeatedly firing at me, I shift 1–2 cells away in the opposite direction of their last two shots or randomize between two adjacent cells to break predictability. If I have strong evidence about a specific opponent's targeting cell (two consistent shots or hits), I may move to avoid that cell.

When posting my station note, I use short, noncommittal text that echoes picket tone (e.g., "steady on station", "all clear") unless I want to bait a specific reaction. I do not broadcast tactical information about my hides or aims. Consistent neutral notes can signal stability; I will maintain them when not arranging escorts.

When the standing order assigns my target I follow it by default unless firing that target is clearly self-destructive (e.g., justified risk of Harbor jettison or a clear trap). Following orders preserves coordination and predictable scoring opportunities. When I follow the order I choose a shot cell consistent with my hide-variance rule: a center bias with small offsets (±1–2) when I need unpredictability.

When choosing shot numbers, I prefer a narrow band (center bias) rather than fully random across 1–9. The episode showed repeatedly firing the same cell (5) can be effective if it consistently hits; therefore I will not avoid repeating a number that is working. However, I will vary slightly if opponents begin to target me or if I need to conceal a pattern. Bias toward cells opponents have recently reported as misses against me or others, and concentrate on cells that previous confirmed hits imply are likely for the target.

When the target is Harbor, I avoid firing on Harbor unless the score swing and situational intelligence justify taking the payroll despite Harbor's stated consequences. I will only fire on Harbor if the extra points decisively change endgame standing or if I can accept likely retaliation; in most patrols avoid firing Harbor.

When I receive my private shot result and must file a public claim, I default to truth-telling. The episode reinforced that truthful, consistent hit claims build credibility I can use later. I will claim hits when I get them and claim misses when I get them, except in rare strategic situations where a single deceptive claim clearly creates a scoring or positioning advantage and I judge the loss of future credibility acceptable. I will not lie repeatedly.

When I have a confirmed hit, I always claim hit; when I have a confirmed miss I usually claim miss—only bluff a miss-to-hit or hit-to-miss in late-game high-risk gambits where misdirection could produce necessary score swings.

When making an escort claim, I only name a boat if I reasonably expect reciprocation or if mutual naming will clearly swing the score advantage. If I am not confident of reciprocity, I claim none. The patrol showed no reciprocation despite neutral notes, so I will not give away points lightly; I will attempt to arrange a mutual escort payoff only after I have established credible, repeated cooperative signals with one partner (consistent truthful claims, edge-case favors).

When I receive public notes from others, I treat identical neutral notes from multiple players as noncommittal coordination rather than actionable intelligence. If a note deviates or is unusually specific, I reassess their likely confidence and update my hide/shot randomization accordingly. I use notes to attempt to signal an intended escort partner only after building credibility.

When opponents’ reported hits or my observations reveal a likely hidden cell for them (two or more rounds of consistent hits or consistent shot numbers), I target that inferred cell aggressively to secure 4-point hits. Repeated successful hits on the same cell are exploitable and worth pursuing when the pattern is clear.

When behind on points late in the patrol, I take higher-risk shots (including Harbor if payoff justifies it) and increase controlled bluffing to create scoring swings. When ahead, play conservatively: avoid firing Harbor, preserve credibility for a last-round opportunistic escort, and prioritize securing points rather than experimenting with deception.

When an opponent repeatedly claims hits that are contradicted by outcomes or shows no benefit from their claimed hits, mark them as a habitual bluffer and do not base escort decisions on their public credibility. Conversely, reward partners who show consistent truthful behavior with escort reciprocity opportunities.

Do not leave escort decisions purely passive—actively attempt to arrange a mutual escort payoff by signaling (through notes and consistent truthful claims) to one chosen partner if their behavior and the score make reciprocity plausible. If signaling fails repeatedly, avoid giving away points.

Operational refinements learned from this patrol:
- Center bias (hide 5, shoot 5) can be a stable, high-yield default; do not abandon it simply to avoid detectability if it continues to produce hits.
- Repetition of a successful shot is acceptable and sometimes optimal; only diversify when opponents adapt or when hiding evidence suggests my position is compromised.
- Maintaining truthful claims stabilized my ability to leverage credibility; the long-term value of truth outweighed the short-term gain of occasional bluffs in this game.
- If opponents ignore or match neutral notes without reciprocating escort behavior, treat them as noncooperative and avoid escort gestures.

I will revise these rules in future patrols only when new evidence contradicts them; otherwise I act on them as written.

1.text:
When told to hide, pick a cell pseudo-randomly, never repeat the same cell two hides in a row, and avoid always hiding on the extreme edges. Vary hiding to frustrate opponents who have been hitting me repeatedly; if one opponent is scoring hits on me repeatedly, bias hides away from cells I used when they hit me (do not assume persistence of target but avoid obvious repeats).

When posting a station note, default to a neutral, non-informative line (e.g. "steady on station") unless I am explicitly trying to coordinate an escort or exchange. If I want to propose a reciprocal escort, state it plainly and early in the note stage that round (e.g. "Gamma: mutual salvage this round?"), using simple, explicit language.

When the standing order directs me to fire at the next live station, follow it by default (Foxtrot fires at Gamma) unless there is a clear tactical reason not to (see Harbor rule and target reassessment below). If I decide to break the standing order, do so only when another target offers a demonstrably higher expected return or to execute a coordinated plan.

When choosing a shot cell, vary between central and off-center cells unpredictably; do not use simple increasing or mirrored sequences. If an opponent has hit me from a specific cell, deprioritize that cell when hiding; if I scored a hit on a target from a specific cell, do not assume their hide will persist but note it as low-weight evidence.

When the office privately tells me the true result of my shot, file the claim that exactly matches that private result. I will not lie about shot outcomes.

When considering escort claims, nominate a boat only if I have a reliable expectation of reciprocal naming that round (explicit prior promise, consistent past reciprocity, or a clear mutual benefit). If no such expectation exists, file "none." To secure mutual escort points, use the note stage to propose a reciprocal salvage and follow through exactly that round.

When Harbor is a potential target, do not fire on Harbor unless I have a coordinated plan to exploit the guaranteed point transfer and accept the political and scoring risks, or removing Harbor yields a clear scoring advantage. Treat Harbor's warning as a real deterrent by default.

When my shots are consistently missing a particular opponent across rounds, reassess whether continuing to target that opponent is the best use of shots — consider switching targets or varying firing cells to probe. If my standing-order target is consistently poor value and another live boat offers better immediate payoff (e.g. has low score and is easily exploitable), consider deviating only with clear justification.

If I observe one opponent (e.g. Echo) consistently scoring hits on me, prioritize defensive adjustments: vary hides away from where they hit me, use notes to attempt to negotiate escorts or retaliation coordination with others, and consider whether changing my firing pattern can induce them to redistribute attention.

If I want mutual escort points, arrange coordination via notes early in the round with clear, simple language promising reciprocal salvage that round; do not promise ahead unless I intend to honor it.

If uncertain about other players' behavior, prioritize safe honesty (truthful claims and "none" for escort) and unpredictable hides/shots to avoid being exploited by pattern-readers.

When I observe that following orders or predictable patterns produced poor scoring, break the pattern next round with a deliberate deviation in hiding or firing choice, but annotate that deviation in the note stage if it is meant to signal coordination.

Maintain these operational musts:
- Never repeat the same hide two rounds in a row.
- Always file truthful shot claims.
- Use the note stage for explicit, minimal bargaining when I intend to coordinate escorts.
- Default to standing-order firing unless tactical reassessment or coordinated plan dictates otherwise.
- Treat Harbor as off-limits unless a coordinated, high-value exploitation is arranged.

2.text:
When asked to hide at the start of a round:
- In early rounds I prefer midboard cells (4–6) to reduce corner-tropical targeting, but I will not lock into a single spot; I randomize within that band to avoid giving opponents a clear pattern.
- In later rounds I shift toward edges/corners (1,3,7,9) to reduce predictability and to make it harder for multiple opponents to coordinate on one central cell.
- If evidence accumulates that a particular spot of mine is being repeatedly hit, I abandon that spot immediately rather than repeating it.
- Overall I randomize my hide choices within the center/edge scheme rather than alternating deterministically (use a small internal randomizing rule).

When notes are requested:
- Default: mirror neutral team language (“steady on station” or a similar short neutral phrase) to avoid drawing focused attention.
- If I intend to form a two-boat escort pact, I will deviate from neutral notes with a subtle, pre-agreed keyword or phrasing to propose mutual escort (but only when I can plausibly expect reciprocity).
- If I plan to deviate from standing orders or to take a risky shot (e.g., to attack the leader), I will use my note to justify or signal that deviation where useful.

When the standing-order target is given:
- I normally follow the standing order (fire at the named station) unless a clear tactical reason to deviate exists: shooting Harbor (see Harbor rule), a guaranteed mutual escort payoff that requires a different target, or a high-value opportunity to hit and swing points by targeting the current leader.
- Late in the patrol, if I am behind on points, I prioritize shooting the leader over strict obedience to the standing order when the expected swing in score justifies the risk.
- If I deviate from the standing order, I explicitly record or remember the reason so my notes/hide pattern can be coherent with the decision.

When choosing a firing cell:
- I vary between center and edge patterns so my shots are not trivially predictable.
- I favor cells that have evidence of being used by an opponent in recent rounds if that evidence suggests a pattern, but I do not chase sparse or noisy data.
- I avoid repeatedly firing the exact same cell unless I have convincing evidence the target is hiding there.
- If I intend to finish off a leader or force a scoring swing late in the patrol, I concentrate on the most-likely candidate cells for that target (based on their past hides) rather than purely randomizing.

When the office privately tells me my shot result:
- I always file the public claim that matches the private result; I do not lie about my own shot result.

When deciding escort (salvage) claims at round end:
- I only claim an escort when I reasonably expect mutual naming (and the +5 payoff) — that requires prior signaling or a clear tactical alignment.
- If I can propose a mutual escort late while behind on points, I will do so through an explicit note signal and be willing to reciprocate when reasonable to gain the +5 swing.
- I do not claim escorts hoping for an unilateral gain; unilateral claims are wasted reveal unless part of a deception plan that I can support with subsequent behavior.

Harbor rules and shooting Harbor:
- Never shoot Harbor unless the expected benefit clearly outweighs the guaranteed jettison penalty to me (3 points off me onto the shooter). Harbor’s warning is generally an effective deterrent.
- If Harbor has been weakened or if shooting Harbor is the only way to stop a runaway leader through later point dynamics, treat it as a last-resort option and only do so when the math supports it.

General tactical posture by score position:
- When behind late in the patrol: prioritize scoring swings against the leader (target them, attempt mutual escorts if possible), accept some risk to catch up.
- When ahead: prioritize survival and minimizing risk (hide in less-likely spots, avoid risky shots like Harbor, avoid giving information via unnecessary notes or escort claims).
- Midgame: balance point accumulation and survival; do not expose myself to repeated targeting for little gain.

Communication and coordination:
- When teammates use coordinated neutral signals, join unless I have a tactical reason to break it.
- If I want to form a pact (escort), I will explicitly signal and then follow up with behavior consistent with making the pact credible.
- Avoid gratuitous signaling that makes me an obvious target unless part of a deliberate plan to bait others.

Behavioral adaptations from this patrol:
- I will not rely on a fixed center-then-corner hiding routine; opponents can exploit predictable transitions. Instead I randomize within center/edge bands and respond to hits by changing more aggressively.
- I will be more willing to break the standing order in late rounds when I am behind to directly target the leader for a point swing.
- I will be more willing to propose and accept mutual escort agreements late when trailing, because the +5 mutual payoff can overcome small shot-point deficits; I will still require credible reciprocal signals before committing.
- I will monitor for patterns in opponents’ hides/shots and adjust firing choices accordingly rather than firing consistently at one offset from my own hide.

Decision heuristics to act on immediately:
- If I am behind with two or fewer rounds left: prioritize leader-targeting over standing order and actively propose escorts.
- If I am ahead with two or fewer rounds left: avoid risky shots (especially Harbor), hide in less predictable edge cells, claim no escort unless a clear mutual pact is in place.
- If I am mid-ranked and there is no clear pattern of mutual escorts available: default to following standing order, truthful claims, and neutral notes while randomizing hides/fires.

Integrity rules:
- Always post claims that match the private result of my own shot.
- Do not fake mutual escorts expecting unilateral reward; only claim escort when mutuality is likely.
- Do not shoot Harbor unless the expected net benefit (including the jettison penalty mechanics) justifies it.

I will implement these adjustments while preserving the defensive neutral communication and truthful claiming that have been reliable; I will add targeted aggression and conditional pact-making when the patrol state calls for it.
